title: The psychology of attention
filename: A little introduction to your mind

slides.title: Your mind has a filter.
slides.body: Selective attention lets you focus on one thing while the rest of the world carries on. Like hearing your name in a crowded room.

slides.title: One thing at a time.
slides.body: What feels like multitasking is usually task switching. Each switch has a cost: a little time, a little accuracy, a little energy.

slides.title: Notice what you notice.
slides.body: Bottom-up attention follows what is loud or new. Top-down attention follows your intentions. A good study space helps the second one win.

slides.title: Give your mind a moment.
slides.body: Sustained attention gets harder over time. Short breaks can help you return to the work with a fresh pair of eyes.
slides.kicker: REST IS PART OF THE PROCESS

slides.title: Memory is a process.
slides.body: Encoding brings information in. Storage keeps it available. Retrieval brings it back when you need it.

slides.title: Make room for the new.
slides.body: Working memory holds a small amount of information for a short time. Group related ideas into chunks to make them easier to handle.

slides.title: Connect the dots.
slides.body: New ideas are easier to remember when you connect them to something you already know. Ask yourself: what does this remind me of?

slides.title: Forgetting is natural.
slides.body: Without practice, memories become harder to retrieve. A little review over time is more useful than one very long session.

slides.title: Sleep on it.
slides.body: Sleep supports memory consolidation. A rested mind has a better chance of keeping what you worked so hard to learn.
slides.kicker: LET YOUR BRAIN DO ITS THING

slides.title: Try to remember first.
slides.body: Close your notes and explain the idea in your own words. Retrieving a memory helps make it easier to retrieve again.

slides.title: Space it out.
slides.body: Revisit a topic across several days. Leave enough time that remembering takes a little effort, then come back again.

slides.title: Mix things up.
slides.body: Practising different types of problems together helps you learn when to use each approach, not just how to repeat it.

slides.title: Familiar is not learned.
slides.body: Recognising a sentence is easier than explaining its meaning. Test what you can recall without the slide in front of you.

slides.title: Start with a small goal.
slides.body: Choose one section and one clear intention. A small finish line makes it easier to begin and to notice your progress.

slides.title: Make space to focus.
slides.body: Put distractions out of reach. Keep the material you need close. Give your attention fewer decisions to make.

slides.title: Be honest with yourself.
slides.body: Save the slides that feel uncertain. They are useful signals about where a little more attention will make the biggest difference.
slides.kicker: A SECOND LOOK IS A GOOD THING

slides.title: A little, often.
slides.body: The best study routine is one you can return to. Keep it gentle, keep it regular, and let small sessions add up.
